videos.summary: Agarwal frames engineering as a stack of abstractions, then shows how the lumped matter discipline reduces Maxwell's equations to lumped elements, demonstrates V-I curves of several devices and where the model breaks down, and derives KVL.

videos.summary: Builds an inspection-based method for sketching first-order RC step responses from initial value, final value and time constant, then uses it to compute the rising and falling delays of an inverter loaded by a gate capacitance. Ends with a crosstalk story and demo showing why faster edges can cause glitches on neighboring pins.

videos.summary: A guest lecturer recasts the RC response in terms of state, splitting it into zero-state and zero-input parts, then uses capacitor charge storage to build a memory cell. The cell is refined from a DRAM-style switch and capacitor into buffered and feedback-based static memory, closing with a small decoded four-bit memory.

videos.summary: Introduces the operational amplifier as an abstraction with an ideal circuit model (huge gain, infinite input resistance, zero output resistance) and shows its unreliable open-loop gain on a scope. A non-inverting amplifier is then analyzed to show that negative feedback makes the gain depend only on resistor ratios, with anti-lock brakes as an analogy.

videos.summary: After wrapping up the op amp oscillator by using it as a clock that discretizes time, the lecture turns to energy and power: it derives static power for a resistive path and shows that charging and discharging a capacitor costs CV^2 per cycle. These combine into static plus CV^2f dynamic power for an inverter, demonstrated with a power meter and a chip-scale estimate.

videos.summary: Shows that the resistive-load NMOS inverter would make a 100-million-gate chip dissipate an absurd static power, then motivates and introduces the PFET and the CMOS inverter, which removes the supply-to-ground path and speeds up rising edges. Closes with CV^2f scaling, supply reduction, clock gating, leakage, and a demo that overheats a CMOS inverter.
